t:
(a) 
Effective the date of enactment of this Act, the Pharmacy Corps and the Medical Administrative Corps are abolished.
 
    (b) Effective the date of enactment of this Act, persons holding temporary appointments or commissions in the Army of the United States permanently assigned or detailed to the Medical Administrative Corps, the Pharmacy Corps, or the Sanitary Corps, shall be automatically transferred and permanently assigned or detailed, as the case may be, to the Medical Service Corps, Regular Army, established by this Act, in the same temporary grade and rank held by them at such time.
 
    (c) The Secretary of War is authorized to prescribe from time to time such regulations as may be necessary for the administration of title I of this Act.
 
    (d) No back pay shall accrue to any person by reason of the enactment hereof.
 
    (e) Effective the date of enactment of this Act, all laws and parts of laws, insofar as they are inconsistent with or in conflict with the provisions of title I of this Act, are repealed.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that this is a purely internal Army reorganization (abolishing corps, transferring personnel) with no outside party involved, so the answer should be No. However, subsection (c) authorizes the Secretary of War to prescribe regulations, and under the definition a grant of rulemaking authority counts as participation even when it is discretionary. The label is less certain because these regulations concern internal military administration and no comment or consultation process is stated.
fable.s: The Secretary of War is authorized to prescribe from time to time such regulations as may be necessary for the administration of title I of this Act.

qwen_block.w: This section describes the abolition of military corps, the transfer of personnel, and the authority of the Secretary of War to prescribe internal regulations. It does not involve consultation with, or participation by, any parties outside the federal government (such as the public, states, or private entities). The regulatory authority mentioned is an internal executive function, not a participatory process.
qwen_block.s: (c) The Secretary of War is authorized to prescribe from time to time such regulations as may be necessary for the administration of title I of this Act.

opus.w: Subsection (c) gives a federal agency head authority to issue regulations. Under the definition and Example 6, rulemaking authority counts as participation, even when the agency can choose whether to use it. The tempting 'No' reading treats the section as purely internal military reorganization, but the grant of regulatory authority is enough to make it 'Yes.'
opus.s: The Secretary of War is authorized to prescribe from time to time such regulations as may be necessary for the administration of title I of this Act.
opus.b:
I'm labelling this **Yes**, mainly because of subsection (c).

1. **The tempting reading, and why it fails.** At first glance this looks like internal Army housekeeping: corps are abolished, officers are moved into the new Medical Service Corps, and conflicting laws are repealed. No outside party is named, so a "No" is tempting. But subsection (c) gives the Secretary of War authority to "prescribe... such regulations." Under the definition, rulemaking counts as participation, and Example 6 treats even optional ("may") authority to regulate as "Yes." One caveat: military personnel rules are often exempt from public notice-and-comment in practice, which is why my confidence is moderate rather than high.

qwen_chat.w: This section authorizes the Secretary of War to prescribe internal regulations for the administration of the Act. It does not require or recommend consultation with, or participation by, any parties outside the federal government. The only actors mentioned are federal officials and military personnel, who are inside the government.
qwen_chat.s: (c) The Secretary of War is authorized to prescribe from time to time such regulations as may be necessary for the administration of title I of this Act.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "regulations" implies a rulemaking process that could involve public comment. However, the text only authorizes the Secretary to prescribe regulations for internal administration and does not explicitly require or recommend any form of public participation, consultation with outside entities, or public hearings. The actors involved (Secretary of War, Army personnel) are all inside the federal government.
